sections.applicability: Applies when identifying and naming rock types encountered in field investigations or laboratory core examination.

sections.title: Color and Grain Size
sections.summary: Explains how to describe rock color using standardized charts (Munsell, Geological Society of London) and grain size using established criteria. Tables 1-9, 1-10, and 1-11 provide color descriptors and grain-size criteria for igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks. A 10X hand lens may be used for fine-grained rocks.
sections.body:
Rock can be described with respect to basic colors on a rock color chart. The most common chart used for this purpose in the United States is the Munsell rock color chart which includes 115 color chips and works with both wet and dry specimens. Another commonly used system is the one published by the Geological Society of London (1977). This system is based on three descriptors as can be seen in Table 1-9.
Grain size for rock refers to the sizes of the small grains that comprise the rock. Because of the nature of some rocks, a 10X hand lens can be used, if necessary, to examine rock sample. Various grain-size criteria have been established, and no single criteria is standard or used most often. An example of grain-size descriptors for different types of rock are found in Table 1-10. Another criterion presented by FHWA (2017) is also included here in Table 1-11 which is similar to that presented by the Geological Society of London (1977).
key_points: The Munsell rock color chart (115 color chips, wet and dry) is the most commonly used color reference in the United States.
The Geological Society of London (1977) color system uses three descriptors (Table 1-9).
Grain size criteria differ between igneous/metamorphic and sedimentary rocks; no single standard is universally adopted.
A 10X hand lens is recommended for examining fine-grained rock samples.
FHWA (2017) grain-size criteria (Table 1-11) range from Very Fine-Grained (<0.075 mm) to Very Coarse-Grained (>4.75 mm).
tables: Table 1-9 Rock Color Descriptors (Geological Society of London 1977)
Table 1-11 Criteria for Defining Rock Grain Size (after FHWA 2017)
sections.applicability: Applies when documenting rock color and grain size during field logging or laboratory core description.

sections.title: Weathering
sections.summary: Describes how to classify the degree of rock weathering using the ISRM six-grade system (Table 1-12), ranging from Fresh (Grade I) to Residual Soil (Grade VI). Explains that weathering results from exposure to water, temperature changes, and other factors, and that increasing weathering generally reduces rock strength, stiffness, and quality.
sections.body: Weathering is the mechanical or chemical deterioration of rock properties by the exposure to water, temperature changes, among other factors. Rock can be described as fresh, slightly weathered, etc. in accordance with Table 1-12 as indicated by the International Society of Rock Mechanics (ISRM). As the degree of weathering increases, usually the strength, stiffness, and quality of the rock decrease.
key_points: Weathering is mechanical or chemical deterioration caused by water, temperature changes, and other environmental factors.
ISRM six-grade weathering classification (Table 1-12): Fresh (I), Slightly Weathered (II), Moderately Weathered (III), Highly Weathered (IV), Completely Weathered (V), Residual Soil (VI).
Increasing weathering grade generally corresponds to decreasing strength, stiffness, and rock quality.
Residual soil (RS) represents advanced decomposition with complete destruction of rock fabric and structure and large volume change.
sections.applicability: Applies when logging rock cores or exposures to assess weathering state and its potential impact on engineering properties.

sections.title: Discontinuities
sections.summary: Covers the description of rock mass discontinuities including spacing, structural features (bedding/foliation), joint form, dip, surface condition, opening size, and filling. Table 1-13 provides spacing classifications from Very Thickly Bedded (>6 ft) to Very Intensely laminated (<0.25 in) for both macrostructural and microstructural features.
sections.body: The spacing of discontinuities in the rock can be described as close, wide, etc., in accordance with Table 1-13. The structural features of a rock mass can be described as thickly bedded or thinly bedded, in accordance with Table 1-13. Depending on project requirements, the form of joint should be identified as stepped, smooth, undulating, planar, etc. In addition, the dip (in degrees), surface condition (rough, smooth, slickensided), opening size (giving width), and filling (none, sand, clay, breccia, etc.) should also be recorded.
key_points: Discontinuity spacing ranges from Very Widely fractured (>6 ft) to Extremely Close (<0.25 in) per Table 1-13.
Macrostructural features include bedding, foliation, and flow banding; microstructural features include lamination, foliation, and cleavage.
Joint form should be described as stepped, smooth, undulating, or planar depending on project requirements.
Key parameters to record: dip (degrees), surface condition (rough/smooth/slickensided), opening width, and infill material (none, sand, clay, breccia, etc.).
sections.applicability: Applies when characterizing structural discontinuities in a rock mass for stability analysis, tunneling, or foundation design.

sections.title: Hardness
sections.summary: Describes methods for estimating rock hardness using field tests (geologic hammer or knife) and the point load test, with two classification tables. Table 1-14 (Hough 1969) provides five hardness classes (I–V) with compressive strength ranges from >2000 to 10–250 kg/cm². Table 1-15 (ISRM/FHWA 2017) provides a more recent seven-grade system (R0–R6) from Extremely Weak to Extremely Strong Rock.
sections.body: The hardness of rock can be estimated by field tests using a geologic hammer or knife and, in the laboratory, using the point load test in accordance with Table 1-14. The corresponding range of strength values for intact rock is also provided. A more recent grading system presented by the ISRM is presented in Table 1-15.
key_points: Hardness can be estimated in the field with a geologic hammer or knife, or in the lab with a point load test.
Hough (1969) hardness classification (Table 1-14): five classes, Class I (>2000 kg/cm²) to Class V (10–250 kg/cm²).
ISRM/FHWA (2017) relative rock strength (Table 1-15): seven grades R0 (Extremely Weak, 2.5–10.8 kg/cm²) to R6 (Extremely Strong, >2,610 kg/cm²).
R6 can only be chipped with firm blows from the hammer end of a geological hammer.
tables: Table 1-14 Hardness Classification of Intact Rock (Hough 1969)
Table 1-15 Criteria and Descriptions for Relative Rock Strength (after FHWA 2017)
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating intact rock strength in the field or laboratory as part of rock mass characterization.

sections.title: Classification by Field and Laboratory Measurements
sections.summary: Parent section covering quantitative rock classification methods based on field and laboratory measurements, including Rock Quality Designation (RQD), uniaxial compressive strength with modulus ratio, and slake durability testing. These measurements supplement visual classification and are used to assign engineering quality ratings to rock.
key_points: Quantitative classification supplements visual description with measurable parameters.
Key methods include RQD (core logging), strength classification (uniaxial compression and point load test), and durability testing (slake durability).
Results are used to assign rock mass quality ratings and support design decisions.
sections.applicability: Applies when field and laboratory measurements are available to quantitatively classify rock quality and strength for engineering design.

sections.title: Rock Quality Designation
sections.summary: Defines the Rock Quality Designation (RQD) index for NX core samples: sum of core pieces ≥4 inches divided by total run length, multiplied by 100. Explains treatment of natural vs. drilling-induced fractures and provides Table 1-16 correlating RQD and velocity index to rock mass quality from Very Poor (0–25%) to Excellent (90–100%).
sections.body: The Rock Quality Designation (RQD) is only for NX size core samples and is computed by summing the lengths of all pieces of core equal to or longer than 4 inches and dividing by the total length of the coring run. The resultant is multiplied by 100 to get RQD in percent. It is necessary to distinguish between natural fractures and those caused by the drilling or recovery operations. The fresh, irregular breaks should be ignored and the pieces counted as intact lengths. Depending on the engineering requirements of the project, breaks induced along highly anisotropic planes, such as foliation or bedding, may be counted as natural fractures. A qualitative relationship between RQD, velocity index, and rock mass quality is presented in Table 1-16. The velocity index is defined as the square of the ratio of the in situ to laboratory or intact compressional wave velocities.
key_points: RQD applies only to NX size core samples; pieces ≥4 inches are summed and divided by total run length, then multiplied by 100.
Drilling-induced fractures (fresh, irregular breaks) are ignored; only natural fractures count.
Breaks along highly anisotropic planes (foliation, bedding) may be counted as natural fractures depending on project requirements.
Velocity index = (V_field / V_lab)²; correlates with RQD to indicate rock mass quality.
RQD quality ratings (Table 1-16): 0–25% Very Poor, 25–50% Poor, 50–75% Fair, 75–90% Good, 90–100% Excellent.
tables: Table 1-16 Engineering Classification for In situ Rock Quality (Merritt and Coon 1970)
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating NX core samples from rock drilling programs to assess in situ rock mass quality.

sections.title: Classification by Strength
sections.summary: Describes classification of rock by uniaxial compressive strength and modulus ratio (per ASTM D7012) and by point load strength index Is(50) (per ASTM D5731), using Figure 1-4. Defines the point load strength index formula and size correction factor, and notes that Is(50) correlates with direct tensile strength, specific gravity, seismic velocity, elastic modulus, and compressive strength.
sections.body:
The uniaxial compressive strength and modulus ratio can be used to classify rock using the results of ASTM D7012. The strength of intact sample can be used with Figure 1-4 to assign a classification as weak, strong, etc.
The point load strength can also be used to classify rock as indicated in Figure 1-4. Point load strength tests, described in ASTM D5731, are sometimes performed in the field for larger projects where rippability and rock strength are critical design factors. This simple field test can be performed on core samples and irregular rock specimens.
The point load strength index, Is(50), is defined as:

Is(50) = P / (F · d²)   (1-4)

F = De / 50   (1-5)

where:
F = size correction factor,
P = the applied force at failure,
d = the distance between the loaded points, and
De = equivalent core diameter.

This index is related to the direct tensile strength of the rock by a proportionality constant F depending on the size of sample. Useful relationships of point load tensile strength index to other parameters such as specific gravity, seismic velocity, elastic modulus, and compressive strength are readily available in the literature.
key_points: Uniaxial compressive strength and modulus ratio (ASTM D7012) classify intact rock strength using Figure 1-4.
Point load strength index Is(50) (ASTM D5731) can be determined in the field on cores or irregular specimens.
Is(50) = P / (F · d²), with size correction factor F = De/50.
Is(50) correlates with direct tensile strength, specific gravity, seismic velocity, elastic modulus, and compressive strength.
Point load testing is particularly useful for large projects where rippability and rock strength are critical design factors.

equations.description: Point load strength index Is(50) = P / (F · d²), where P is applied force at failure, F is size correction factor, and d is distance between loaded points.
Size correction factor F = De / 50, where De is the equivalent core diameter.

figures: Figure 1-4 Rock Strength Characterization (after Broch and Franklin 1972)
sections.applicability: Applies when classifying intact rock strength using uniaxial compressive strength tests or point load tests, particularly for projects where rippability and rock strength govern design.

sections.title: Classification by Durability
sections.summary: Addresses short-term weathering and durability classification of rocks, particularly shales and mudstones, which can significantly degrade on exposure. Describes the slake durability test (ASTM D4644) and the jar slake test (Santi 1998) as standardized procedures for evaluating weatherability under wetting and drying cycles.
sections.body: Short-term weathering of rocks, particularly shales, and mudstones, can have a considerable effect on their engineering performance. The weatherability of these materials is extremely variable, and rocks that are likely to degrade on exposure should be further characterized by use of tests for durability under standard drying and wetting cycles. The slake durability test is a standardized procedure, described in ASTM D4644, used for this purpose. For example, if wetting and drying cycles reduces the grain size of shale, then rapid slaking and erosion in the field is probable when the rock is exposed. Another method used for this purpose is the jar slake test described by Santi (1998).
key_points: Shales and mudstones are particularly susceptible to short-term weathering and engineering performance degradation.
Slake durability test (ASTM D4644) is the standardized procedure for evaluating rock durability under wetting/drying cycles.
Jar slake test (Santi 1998) is an alternative durability assessment method.
Grain size reduction of shale under wetting/drying cycles indicates probable rapid slaking and erosion in the field.
Durability testing should be applied to any rock that is likely to degrade upon exposure.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating rocks prone to degradation on exposure, especially shales and mudstones, to predict field performance after excavation or exposure.

sections.title: Rock Mass Classification Systems
sections.summary: Introduces three primary rock mass classification systems (Q System, RMR, GSI) and several additional systems summarized in Table 1-17. Emphasizes that classification systems are useful for estimating engineering properties and supporting design methodologies, and that the appropriate system depends on regional practice and project type.
sections.body:
Various classification systems have been developed for classifying rock mass for engineering projects. Three of the main systems are described in this section. The reader is encouraged to check for the classification system used in the region of practice and that most applies to the project in question.
The classification of the rock mass using some of these systems is useful to estimate physical and engineering properties using published values and charts. Also, some design methodologies rely on the classification of the rock mass.
key_points: Three primary systems covered: Q System (Barton et al. 1974), RMR/Geomechanics Classification (Bieniawski 1973), and GSI (Marinos et al. 2007).
Classification results can be used to estimate physical and engineering properties and support design methodologies.
The appropriate classification system depends on regional practice and project-specific requirements.
Additional systems include Rock Structure Rating, Unified Rock Classification, NATM, and Coal Mine Roof Rating (Table 1-17).
sections.applicability: Applies when a formal rock mass quality rating is needed to support engineering design for tunnels, foundations, slopes, or excavations.

sections.title: Q System
sections.summary: Describes the Q System (Barton et al. 1974) for rock mass classification, which quantifies rock quality using RQD, number of joint sets, joint properties, and a stress reduction factor. The Q value can be used to estimate tunnel roof pressure and support requirements, as well as joint properties.
sections.body: Barton et al. (1974) defines the value of Q in terms of RQD, the number of joint sets, the joint properties, and a stress reduction factor. Extensive tables are provided to guide the engineer in the selection of appropriate values. The roof pressure and support requirements for tunnels can be estimated from the value of Q, as well as some of the joint properties.
key_points: Q is defined using RQD, number of joint sets, joint properties, and a stress reduction factor.
Extensive tables guide parameter selection for Q value calculation.
Q value enables estimation of tunnel roof pressure and support requirements.
Particularly suited to tunnel design applications.
sections.applicability: Applies when classifying rock mass quality for tunneling applications where support requirements and roof pressure estimates are needed.

sections.title: Rock Mass Rating System
sections.summary: Describes the Rock Mass Rating (RMR) system, also known as the Geomechanics classification (Bieniawski 1973), which classifies rock based on uniaxial compressive strength, RQD, joint spacing and properties, and groundwater conditions. RMR can be related to stand-up time, unsupported active span length, and roof pressure, though it is not limited to tunneling.
sections.body: The rock mass rating system (RMR), also known as the Geomechanics classification, by Bieniawski (1973) classifies rock based on the uniaxial compressive strength, RQD, the spacing and properties of the joints, and groundwater conditions. While not solely intended for tunneling applications, the RMR can be related to stand-up time, unsupported active span length, and roof pressure.
key_points: RMR parameters: uniaxial compressive strength, RQD, joint spacing and properties, and groundwater conditions.
RMR is not limited to tunneling — applicable to foundations, slopes, and other engineering contexts.
RMR correlates with stand-up time, unsupported active span length, and roof pressure.
Also known as the Geomechanics classification.
sections.applicability: Applies when a multi-parameter rock mass quality rating is needed for tunneling, foundation design, or slope stability evaluation.

sections.title: Geological Strength Index
sections.summary: Describes the Geological Strength Index (GSI, Marinos et al. 2007), a qualitative rock mass quality descriptor closely linked to rock strength and used to estimate rock properties for stability analysis. Covers the GSI selection charts (Figures 1-5 and 1-6), limitations on use, and a modified GSI system for heterogeneous rocks such as layered shales and sandstones.
sections.body:
The Geological Strength Index (GSI) has become a commonly used approach to describe rock mass quality in a qualitative manner (Marinos et al. 2007). Because it is closely linked to rock strength, GSI is most useful as a tool to help estimate rock properties for stability analysis. The GSI can be quantified as indicated in Figure 1-5; however, a range of values should always be used. Such values of GSI may be used as input for empirical equations for the shear strength of a rock mass.
The GSI is most useful for rock masses with many discontinuities that cannot be effectively modeled in direct fashion. According to Marinos et al. (2007), GSI should not be used for (1) rocks with clear discontinuities and well-defined dominant structure, (2) excavated faces in strong, hard rock with discontinuities spaced at similar dimensions to the tunnel or slope, or (3) low strength "young" rocks such as marls, claystones, siltstones, and weak sandstones. Marinos et al. (2007) developed a modified GSI system for heterogeneous rocks, such as layered shales and sandstones, as shown in Figure 1-6. The application of GSI to these rocks should account for their tendency to behave differently at depth compared to near the ground surface.
key_points: GSI qualitatively describes rock mass quality and is closely linked to rock strength; used to estimate properties for stability analysis.
A range of GSI values should always be used, not a single value.
GSI values serve as input for empirical shear strength equations for rock masses.

GSI should NOT be used for: rocks with well-defined dominant structure, excavated faces in strong rock with discontinuity spacing similar to tunnel/slope dimensions, or low-strength 'young' rocks (marls, claystones, siltstones, weak sandstones).
Modified GSI (Figure 1-6) is available for heterogeneous rocks like layered shales and sandstones.
Depth-dependent behavior of heterogeneous rocks must be accounted for when applying GSI.
figures: Figure 1-5 GSI Selection Chart for Jointed Rock (after Marinos et al. 2007)
Figure 1-6 GSI Selection Chart for Heterogeneous Rock (after Marinos et al. 2007)
sections.applicability: Applies when estimating rock mass properties for stability analysis in rock masses with many discontinuities, excluding rocks with well-defined structure or low-strength young rocks.

sections.title: Other Classification Systems
sections.summary: Summarizes five additional rock mass classification systems in Table 1-17, including Rock Structure Rating, Unified Rock Classification, Rock Material Field Classification, New Austrian Tunneling Method, and Coal Mine Roof Rating. Each system has specific intended applications ranging from tunnel support to slope stability and coal mine roof assessment.
sections.body: Some other classification systems have been proposed depending on the region, purpose, and needs. Some of these systems are summarized in Table 1-17.
key_points: Rock Structure Rating (Skinner 1988): tunnel support, excavation, and mining/construction ground support.
Unified Rock Classification (Williamson and Kuhn 1988): foundations, excavation methods, slope stability, blasting, and groundwater transmission.
Rock Material Field Classification (NRCS 2002): shallow excavation, hydraulic erodibility, excavatability, and rock-mass stability.
New Austrian Tunneling Method (Lauffer 1997): cyclical and TBM tunneling with design extended into construction via monitoring.
Coal Mine Roof Rating (Molinda and Mark 1994): bedded coal-measure rocks and structural competence influenced by discontinuities.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting an alternative rock mass classification system for specialized applications such as mining, coal mine roof assessment, or hydraulic erodibility evaluation.

sections.title: Special Materials
sections.summary: Container section introducing special soil materials that require particular engineering consideration. All substantive content is contained within subsections, beginning with expansive soils in 1-5.1.
key_points: Covers soil types with atypical engineering behavior requiring special treatment.
Subsection 1-5.1 addresses expansive soils specifically.
sections.applicability: Applies whenever a project site may contain special soil materials such as expansive soils.

sections.title: Expansive Soils
sections.summary: Container section for expansive soils, covering their characteristics, identification, classification, and laboratory testing. Subsections address the physical behavior, geographic distribution, predictive methods, and standardized test procedures used to evaluate swelling potential.
key_points: Expansive soils pose risks to shallow foundations, roads, and other infrastructure where seasonal moisture variation occurs.
Contains subsections on characteristics (1-5.1.1) and identification/classification (1-5.1.2).
sections.applicability: Applies when projects are sited in areas with potentially expansive soils requiring evaluation of swelling potential and associated design considerations.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.summary: Describes the physical and mineralogical characteristics of expansive soils, including controlling factors for swelling potential and pressure, typical clay minerals (montmorillonite, vermiculite), observable field indicators, seasonal cracking behavior, the concept of the active zone, and the geographic distribution of highly expansive soils in the United States.
sections.body:
Expansive soils are distinguished by their potential for excessive volume increase upon access to moisture. The swelling potential and the magnitude of the swelling pressure are controlled by the clay minerals contained in the soil, the structure and fabric of the soil, overburden pressure, and other physical-chemical aspects of the soil (Holtz et al. 2011). These soils usually contain montmorillonite and vermiculite clay minerals.

Expansive soils are characterized by a very high dry strength and high plasticity, are often shiny when cut with a knife, and are very weak when wet (Holtz et al. 2011). These soils usually form deep cracks during the dry season and expand closing the gaps creating a homogenous appearance during the wet season.

Even though expansive soils can be encountered at great depth, they are mainly a problem at shallow depths where the effect of variations in water content is greater (FHWA 2017). The zone affected by seasonal variation in water content is also called the active zone for expansive soils. This is very important when designing foundations, roads, etc.

According to Holtz et al. (2011) expansive soils can be found around the world. In the United States, the regions with the greatest occurrence of highly expansive soils are North and South Dakota, Montana, eastern Wyoming, eastern Colorado, the Four Corners Region, California, and east Texas. Figure 1-7 illustrates the distribution of expansive soils throughout the United States.
key_points: Swelling potential and pressure are controlled by clay mineralogy, soil structure and fabric, overburden pressure, and physical-chemical properties.
Montmorillonite and vermiculite are the clay minerals most commonly associated with expansive soils.
Field indicators include very high dry strength, high plasticity, shiny cut surfaces, weak wet behavior, and deep desiccation cracks in the dry season.
The active zone is the shallow depth range most affected by seasonal water content variation — critical for foundation and pavement design.
Highest occurrence in the US: North/South Dakota, Montana, eastern Wyoming, eastern Colorado, Four Corners Region, California, and east Texas.
sections.applicability: Applies during preliminary site reconnaissance and subsurface investigation planning in regions where expansive soils are known or suspected to occur.

sections.title: Identification and Classification
sections.summary: Covers methods for identifying expansive soils and predicting swelling potential, including field observation of cracks, clay mineral identification techniques (x-ray diffraction, DTA, CEC, electron microscopy), plasticity-based classification tables, the IBC 2018 four-criteria definition, and the ASTM D4829 Expansion Index test procedure with the EI formula and classification table.
sections.body:
Expansive soils can be identified in various ways, and their swelling potential can be nominally predicted. Expansive soils can sometimes be identified during visits to a project site by looking for cracks in nearby structures or desiccation cracks in the soil surface. Another method is identifying the clay minerals in the soil. If the soil has highly expansive clay minerals (e.g. montmorillonite), that is a good indication that the soil could be expansive. Some of the methods that can be used to identify clay minerals are x-ray diffraction, differential thermal analyses, cation exchange capacity, and electron microscopy.

Soil plasticity is often used to identify expansive soils. As the plasticity index or liquid limit of the soils increases, the potential for swelling upon contact with water also tend to increase. Dakshanamurthy and Raman (1973) presented the method shown in Table 1-18 to infer the swelling potential based on the liquid limit. The information presented in Table 1-19 and Figure 1-8 provides another method of assessing the potential for volume change of a given soil.

The International Building Code 2018 (ICC 2018) considers a soil to be expansive if these four criteria are met:
1) Plasticity index equal or greater than 15 as determined using ASTM D4318,
2) More than 10% of soil particles passing a No. 200 (75 μm) sieve, as determined using ASTM D6913 or D1140,
3) More than 10% of soil particles are less than 5 μm in size, as determined using ASTM D7928, and
4) Expansion index is greater than 20, as determined using ASTM D4829 (described below).
If the soil shows compliance with Item 4, it is not necessary to show compliance with Items 1 through 3.

Two laboratory tests have standardized procedures to measure the swelling potential of soils. In the Expansion Index test (ASTM D4829), the soil is compacted in a rigid mold at a water content and unit weight that gives a degree of saturation of 50% ± 2%. A vertical confining pressure of 1 psi is applied to the specimen before the specimen is submerged in distilled water, and the deformation of the specimen is recorded for 24 hours or until the rate of deformation is below 0.0002 inch/hour, whichever occur first with a minimum recording time of 3 hours. This test is used to obtain the expansion index of the soil, defined as follows:

EI = (ΔH / Hi) × 1000

where,
EI = expansion index,
ΔH = change in height during the test, and
Hi = initial height of the test specimen.

According to ASTM D4829, the expansion index can be used to estimate the swelling potential of soils as described in Table 1-20.
key_points: Field identification cues include desiccation cracks in soil and cracks in nearby structures; laboratory clay mineral identification uses x-ray diffraction, DTA, CEC, and electron microscopy.
Higher plasticity index and liquid limit correlate with greater swelling potential; Table 1-18 classifies swelling by liquid limit ranges.
Table 1-19 and Figure 1-8 provide classification-based expansion potential assessment using colloidal content, plasticity index, and shrinkage limit.
IBC 2018 defines expansive soil by four criteria: PI ≥ 15, >10% passing No. 200 sieve, >10% particles < 5 μm, and EI > 20 (ASTM D4829); compliance with criterion 4 alone is sufficient.
ASTM D4829 Expansion Index test: specimen compacted to 50% ± 2% saturation, loaded at 1 psi, submerged in distilled water, deformation monitored for 24 hours or until rate < 0.0002 in/hr.
EI = (ΔH / Hi) × 1000; classified from Very Low (0–20) to Very High (>130) per Table 1-20.

equations.description: Expansion Index (EI) formula: EI = (ΔH / Hi) × 1000, where ΔH is the change in specimen height during the ASTM D4829 test and Hi is the initial specimen height.

sections.applicability: Applies when identifying and classifying expansive soils during site investigation, laboratory testing, or design verification against building code requirements.

sections.title: Collapsing Soils
sections.summary: Introduces collapsing soils as a category of problematic soils that undergo large volume decreases upon wetting without increased external load. Covers characteristics, identification methods, and classification approaches. Serves as a container for subsections on characteristics (1-5.2.1) and identification/classification (1-5.2.2).
key_points: Collapsing soils undergo large volume decrease upon wetting without increase in external load.
Common examples include loess, weakly cemented sands/silts with soluble cementing agents, and certain granite residual soils.
Deposits are typically associated with arid or semi-arid regions of moisture deficiency.
Identification during subsurface investigation is critical so remediation or design accommodations can be made.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating sites with potential collapsible soil conditions, particularly in arid or semi-arid regions.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.summary: Describes the defining characteristics of collapsible soils, including structural, mineralogical, and environmental features. Details the four necessary conditions for collapse per FHWA (2017): open/partially saturated fabric, sufficient total stress, bonding agents or negative pore pressures, and addition of water. Discusses the dependency of collapse magnitude on soil composition, density, water content, and confining stress.
sections.body:
Collapsing soils are distinguished by their potential to undergo large decrease in volume upon increase in moisture content without an increase in external loading. When dry, these soils are stable and able to support significant structural loads. Examples of soils exhibiting this behavior are loess, weakly cemented sands and silts where cementing agent is soluble (e.g., soluble gypsum, halite, etc.), and certain granite residual soils. A common feature of collapsible soils is loose bulky grains held together by capillary stresses. Collapsible soils are also characterized by loss of strength when wetted, low density, moisture sensitivity, and the presence of gypsum or anhydrite. Deposits of collapsible soils are usually associated with regions of moisture deficiency (arid or semi-arid regions). According to FHWA (2017), the following conditions are necessary for collapse to occur:
1) an open, and partially saturated and unstable fabric,
2) enough total stress to make the soil structure metastable,
3) existence of a bonding agent or negative pore pressures to create a metastable structure, and
4) addition of water to destroy the metastable structure.
The collapse of soils supporting structures can cause significant damage as a result of total and differential settlement. The magnitude of the collapse depends on factors, such as the soil composition, dry density, water content, confining stress, and the agent causing the metastable structure. For this reason, it is important to identify collapsible soils during the subsurface investigation so they can be remediated or considered in the design phase.
key_points: Collapsible soils lose volume upon wetting without additional external load; they are stable when dry and can support significant loads.
Common collapsible soil types: loess, weakly cemented sands/silts with soluble cements (gypsum, halite), and certain granite residual soils.
Key feature: loose bulky grains held by capillary stresses; also characterized by low density, moisture sensitivity, and presence of gypsum or anhydrite.
Four conditions necessary for collapse per FHWA (2017): open/partially saturated fabric, sufficient total stress, bonding agent or negative pore pressures, and addition of water.
Collapse magnitude depends on soil composition, dry density, water content, confining stress, and the metastable-structure-causing agent.
Collapsible soil deposits are typically found in arid or semi-arid regions with moisture deficiency.
sections.applicability: Applies when characterizing soil behavior in arid or semi-arid environments where collapsible soil conditions may be present.

sections.title: Identification and Classification
sections.summary: Presents methods to identify and classify collapsible soils. References Holtz et al. (2011) using USBR data (Figure 1-9) showing collapse potential increases with decreasing liquid limit and in situ dry density. Also references Ayadat and Hanna (2007b) design charts (Figure 1-10) for assessing collapse potential using uniformity coefficient, water content, and dry unit weight, and Ayadat and Hanna (2007a) fall cone method.
sections.body:
One method to identify the potential of soils to collapse is presented by Holtz et al. (2011) using data from the USBR and is shown in Figure 1-9. From this figure, the potential for collapse increases with decreasing liquid limit and in situ dry density.
Ayadat and Hanna (2007b) presented a detailed study on the potential of collapse of soil. In this study, they investigated the effect of the uniformity coefficient, water content, and dry unit weight on the collapse potential. Figure 1-10 was presented as a method to assess the potential for a soil to be collapsible along with a detailed method to estimate the strain caused by collapsing for different soils. Ayadat and Hanna (2007a) also presented a method to assess the potential for a soil to be collapsible using the fall cone apparatus (Section 3-2.4.2.6).
key_points: Collapse potential increases with decreasing liquid limit and decreasing in situ dry density (Holtz et al. 2011, USBR data, Figure 1-9).
Ayadat and Hanna (2007b) design charts (Figure 1-10) assess collapse potential using uniformity coefficient, water content, and dry unit weight.
Figure 1-10 also provides a method to estimate collapse-induced strain for different soils.
Ayadat and Hanna (2007a) provide an alternative identification method using the fall cone apparatus (Section 3-2.4.2.6).
figures: Figure 1-9 Collapsibility Based on In situ Dry Density and Liquid Limit (after Holtz et al. 2011)
Figure 1-10 Design Charts for Predicting Collapse Behavior of Soils (after Ayadat and Hanna 2007b)
sections.applicability: Applies when screening or classifying soils in the field or laboratory for collapse potential during subsurface investigation.

sections.title: Frost Susceptibility and Permafrost
sections.summary: Container section covering frost susceptibility of soils and permafrost conditions. Addresses the physical mechanisms of frost heave, identification of frost-susceptible soils, classification systems, and implications for structures including pavements, shallow foundations, and utilities in freezing climates.
key_points: Frost susceptibility and permafrost are major geotechnical hazards in cold climates, requiring special design and construction considerations.
Two subtopics are covered: physical characteristics of frost action and permafrost, and identification/classification of frost-susceptible soils.
sections.applicability: Applies to any project site subject to seasonal freezing or located in permafrost regions.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.summary: Describes the physical mechanisms of frost action in soils. Non-frost-susceptible soils experience ~4% volume increase on freezing. Frost-susceptible soils develop ice lenses causing greater, non-uniform heave. Thawing causes trapped water, soil softening, and loss of support — often more damaging than heave itself. Permafrost definition and construction challenges are also introduced.
sections.body:
In non-frost susceptible soil, a typical volume increase due to ground freezing is about 4%. This volume increase is caused by the increase in water volume as it freezes. In soils susceptible to frost, soil heave is much greater as water flows to colder zones forming ice lenses. The formation of ice lenses typically is not uniform, meaning that the increase in volume is not evenly distributed throughout a site and can cause distress to structures. During warmer weather, the soil and ice lenses will tend to thaw from the top down. Water can become trapped in the soil near the surface, leading to an increase in water content and softening of the soil. The associated loss of support can be even more detrimental to structures than the frost heave itself. This is specially a problem for pavement structures and structures supported on shallow foundations, as well as utilities, if not buried well below the depth of freezing.

Permafrost refers to a thick top layer of soil that stays frozen throughout the year. Permafrost particularly occurs in the Northern Hemisphere, including Canada and Alaska. Construction in permafrost is very challenging and requires special considerations during design and construction.
key_points: Non-frost-susceptible soils expand ~4% on freezing due to the volumetric expansion of water alone.
Frost-susceptible soils experience much greater heave driven by water migration to colder zones and formation of ice lenses.
Ice lens formation is non-uniform, causing differential heave and structural distress.
During thaw, water becomes trapped near the surface, softening the soil and reducing bearing capacity — potentially more damaging than the heave itself.
Pavements, shallow foundations, and utilities are especially vulnerable to frost heave and thaw weakening.
Permafrost is a year-round frozen soil layer common in Canada and Alaska; construction there requires special design and construction measures.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating frost action risks for structures, pavements, and utilities in sites subject to seasonal freezing or permafrost conditions.

sections.title: Identification and Classification
sections.summary: Covers identification of frost-susceptible soils and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers frost design soil classification system. Frost penetration less than ~0.30 m is generally not a concern. Silts are most susceptible; SM, ML, GM, SC, GC, and CL soils also have susceptibility. Table 1-21 classifies soils from NFS through F4 using USCS classification and percent finer than 0.02 mm. Figure 1-12 relates laboratory heave rates to fines content.
sections.body:
Problematic frost action requires both frost penetration into the ground and frost susceptible soils. According to Holtz et al. (2011), if the frost penetration during the worst part of the winter is less than about 0.30 m, frost heave should not be of concern to structures. The maximum depths of frost penetration in the United States are shown in Figure 1-11. These depths are for extremely cold winters without much snow cover. Snow cover, especially early in the winter, will decrease the frost depth significantly. Silts are the most susceptible to frost heave, but most soils with some fines content have also some susceptibility to freezing. This includes soils classifying as SM, ML, GM, SC, GC, and CL. Holtz et al. (2011) presented the information shown in Table 1-21 summarizing a design classification system for frost susceptible soils. This system uses the soil classification system and the percent of soil finer than 0.02 mm (8x10-4 inches) to assess the susceptibility to freezing.

Figure 1-12 relates the rate of frost heave to the percent of particles finer than 0.02 mm (8x10-4 inches) based on USCS classification. This figure also includes the susceptibility classification for each type of soil. The information presented in this figure is based on laboratory testing by the U.S. Department of the Army (1984). According to Holtz et al. (2011), these rates are higher than those expected in the field, and soils with a laboratory rate of frost heave of up to 1 mm/day (0.04 inches/day) can be used under pavements, unless severe conditions are expected, but some frost heave should be expected.
key_points: Frost heave is only problematic when frost-susceptible soils AND significant frost penetration (>~0.30 m) coexist.
Figure 1-11 maps maximum frost penetration depths across the continental U.S. for extreme cold winters without snow cover; snow cover reduces actual frost depth.
Silts are the most frost-susceptible soil type; SM, ML, GM, SC, GC, and CL soils also exhibit susceptibility.
The USACE frost design classification (Table 1-21) uses USCS classification and percent finer than 0.02 mm to assign frost groups from NFS (negligible) to F4 (low to very high susceptibility).
Figure 1-12 shows laboratory frost heave rates vs. percent finer than 0.02 mm by USCS group; field rates are lower than laboratory rates.
Soils with laboratory heave rates up to 1 mm/day (0.04 in/day) may be used under pavements except in severe conditions, though some heave should be anticipated.
figures: Figure 1-11 Maximum Depths (in meters) of Frost Penetration in the Continental United States (NOAA 1978)
Figure 1-12 Rates of Heave in Laboratory Freezing Tests on Remolded Soils (U.S. Department of the Army 1984)
tables: Table 1-21 U.S. Army Corps of Engineers Frost Design Soil Classification
sections.applicability: Applies when identifying and classifying frost-susceptible soils for design of pavements, foundations, and utilities in areas with seasonal frost penetration.

sections.title: Limestone and Related Materials
sections.summary: Covers the engineering significance of limestone, dolomite, gypsum, and anhydrite, focusing on their solubility and the karst features (cavities, sinkholes, pinnacles, fissures) that pose major challenges for foundation design, water-retaining structures, and pavement performance.
key_points: Limestones are defined as rocks composed of >50% carbonate minerals, of which ≥50% are calcite and/or aragonite.
Solubility is the most significant engineering property — it leads to karst geology including caves, channels, and clay-filled features.
Key karst hazards include vertical/horizontal fissures and joints, pinnacles, and sinkholes.
Sinkholes result from soil erosion into karst voids or sudden void collapse and can catastrophically damage structures and pavements.
Near-shore carbonate sediments (marl, chalk) exhibit erratic induration and variable load-supporting capacity.
Subsurface investigation and geophysical techniques are essential for characterizing karst terrain.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing or investigating sites in limestone, dolomite, gypsum, or anhydrite terrain where karst features may be present.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.summary: Describes the defining properties of limestone and related soluble rocks, including their carbonate mineralogy, variability in induration, and the formation of karst features such as solution caves, fissures, pinnacles, and sinkholes that create engineering hazards for foundations and water-retaining structures.
sections.body:
Limestone, dolomite, gypsum, and anhydrite are characterized by their solubility and thus the potential for the presence and/or development of cavities. Limestones are defined as those rocks composed of more than 50% carbonate minerals of which 50% or more consist of calcite and/or aragonite. Some near-shore carbonate sediments (also called limestone, marl, and chalk) could fit this description. Such sediments are noted for erratic degrees of induration, and thus variability in load supporting capacity and uncertainty in their long-term performance under sustained loads. The most significant limestone feature is its solubility. An extremely soluble limestone can contain many solution caves, channels, or other open, water, or clay-filled features. These features are often referred to as karst geology or topography.

Karst features that present important engineering challenges include vertical and horizontal fissures and joints, pinnacles, and sinkholes. Fissures and joints may contain very weak soil and also provide conduits for the flow of water, which are particularly problematic for water retaining structures. Pinnacles are spires or spines of rock left behind by the dissolution process and result in very uneven foundation support. Sinkholes are the result of soil erosion into karst voids or the sudden collapse of voids. Structures and pavements can be catastrophically damaged by sinkholes.
key_points: Limestone = >50% carbonate minerals with ≥50% calcite and/or aragonite; marl and chalk fall under this category.
Solubility is the dominant engineering concern, enabling formation of caves, channels, and clay-filled voids (karst).
Near-shore carbonate sediments show erratic induration and unpredictable long-term load-bearing performance.
Fissures and joints carry weak soil and act as water conduits — critical problem for water-retaining structures.
Pinnacles cause highly uneven foundation support; sinkholes can cause catastrophic structural and pavement damage.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating subsurface conditions at sites underlain by limestone, dolomite, gypsum, or anhydrite for any type of structure or pavement.

sections.title: Identification and Classification
sections.summary: Describes methods for identifying and classifying karstic areas, starting with desk studies and site visits to detect surface expressions such as sinkholes, and progressing to subsurface drilling and geophysical techniques (seismic refraction, resistivity, gravimetry). References USGS karst maps, FHWA 2017 drilling guidance, ASTM D6429, and Figure 1-13 and Table 1-22.
sections.body:
The identification of karstic areas should start by desk studies and site visits to look for surface expressions of solution features. Sinkholes are the surface expression of rock dissolution and can be used to infer that karstic rocks are found in the area. Aerial photos, local geology maps, LIDAR data, etc. are also a useful source of information to identify features that are caused by karstic rocks. A map of the karst and potential karst areas in the United States presented by USGS (2014) is shown here in Figure 1-13.

A subsurface investigation program is very important in karstic areas to better characterize the possible caverns, sinkholes, pinnacles, etc. Drilling is a very powerful tool for this purpose and should be done more extensively in this type of terrain (FHWA 2017). Geophysical techniques, including shallow seismic refraction, resistivity, and gravimetry, are often found to be valuable supplements. The suggested methods by ASTM D6429 to estimate the depth to bedrock and the occurrence of sinkholes and voids is presented in Table 1-22.
key_points: Start karst identification with desk studies: aerial photos, local geology maps, and LIDAR data to detect surface solution features.
Sinkholes at the surface are direct indicators of underlying karstic rock dissolution.
USGS (2014) karst map of the contiguous United States (Figure 1-13) is a key reference for regional identification.
Subsurface drilling should be conducted more extensively in karst terrain than in typical investigations (FHWA 2017).
Geophysical methods — shallow seismic refraction, resistivity, and gravimetry — are valuable supplements to drilling.
ASTM D6429 provides suggested methods for estimating depth to bedrock and locating sinkholes and voids (Table 1-22).
figures: Figure 1-13 Karst and Potential Karst Areas in Soluble Rocks in the Contiguous United States (USGS 2014)
sections.applicability: Applies during the site investigation planning phase for projects located in or near known or suspected karst terrain.

sections.title: Coral and Coral Formation
sections.summary: Introduces coral and coral formations as a distinct soil type found in tropical regions. Covers the general nature of coral reefs, coralline soils as foundation materials, and the broad variability in engineering properties that makes reliance on 'typical properties' inadvisable for preliminary engineering decisions.
key_points: Coral and coralline debris are found in tropical regions where water temperature exceeds 20°C.
Coralline soils are typically thin (a few meters) and form a veneer over cemented materials such as limestones and sandstones.
Extreme variability in engineering properties makes 'typical properties' an unreliable basis for preliminary engineering decisions.
Unconfined compression strengths of intact coral specimens range widely from 50 tsf to 300 tsf.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating coral or coralline formations in tropical regions for any engineering or foundation purpose.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.summary: Describes the physical and engineering characteristics of coral and coralline soils, including their origin, depositional setting, brittleness, susceptibility to solution, and suitability for various foundation types. Notes that heavy structures typically require pile foundations due to erratic induration and that predrilling is frequently needed.
sections.body:
Living coral and coralline debris are generally found in tropical regions where the water temperature exceeds 20°C. Coral is a term commonly used for the group of animals which secrete an outer skeleton composed of calcium carbonate, and which generally grow in colonies. The term coral reef is often applied to large concentrations of such colonies which form extensive submerged tracts around tropical coasts and islands. In general, coralline soils deposited after the breakdown of the reef, typically by wave action, are thin (a few meters thick) and form a veneer upon cemented materials (limestones, sandstones, etc.).

Coralline deposits are generally poor foundation materials in their natural state because of their variability and susceptibility to solution by percolating waters, and their generally brittle nature. Coralline materials are often used for compacted fill for roads and light structures. Under loads, compaction occurs as the brittle carbonate grains fracture and consolidate. They can provide a firm support for mats or spread footings bearing light loads, but it is necessary to thoroughly compact the material before using it as a supporting surface. Heavy structures in coral areas are generally supported on pile foundations because of the erratic induration. Predrilling frequently is required.

Because of extreme variability in engineering properties of natural coral formations, it is not prudent to make preliminary engineering decisions on the basis of "typical properties." Unconfined compression strengths of intact specimens may range from 50 tsf to 300 tsf.
key_points: Coral is found in tropical regions where water temperature exceeds 20°C and consists of calcium carbonate-secreting colonial animals.
Coralline soils are typically thin (a few meters), forming a veneer over cemented materials like limestone and sandstone.
Coralline deposits are poor natural foundation materials due to variability, susceptibility to dissolution by percolating water, and brittleness.
Coralline materials are commonly used as compacted fill for roads and light structures; compaction causes carbonate grain fracture and consolidation.
Mats or spread footings can bear light loads if the material is thoroughly compacted beforehand.
Heavy structures in coral areas typically require pile foundations due to erratic induration; predrilling is frequently necessary.
Unconfined compression strengths of intact coral specimens range from 50 tsf to 300 tsf — 'typical properties' should not guide preliminary decisions.
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing the engineering suitability of natural coral or coralline deposits for foundation design or fill use in tropical regions.

sections.title: Identification and Classification
sections.summary: Describes how coralline and algal materials are identified and classified, noting their biogenic origin and the broad gradation of particle sizes from boulders to fine-grained muds. Also notes the range of particle shapes from sharp and irregular to well-rounded. Coralline deposits are generally referred to as 'biogenic materials.'
sections.body: Because the granular coralline and algal materials are derived from organisms which vary in size from microscopic shells to large coral heads several meters in diameter, the fragments are broadly graded and range in size from boulders to fine-grained muds. Similarly, the shape of these materials varies from sharp, irregular fragments to well-rounded particles. Coralline deposits are generally referred to as "biogenic materials"
key_points: Coralline and algal materials are biogenic, derived from organisms ranging from microscopic shells to coral heads several meters in diameter.
Particle sizes are broadly graded, ranging from boulders down to fine-grained muds.
Particle shapes vary widely, from sharp and irregular fragments to well-rounded particles.
Coralline deposits are generally classified and referred to as 'biogenic materials.'
sections.applicability: Applies when identifying or classifying coral-derived soils in the field or laboratory for engineering assessment.

sections.title: Quick Clays
sections.summary: Overview of quick clays, a sensitive marine clay type prone to dramatic strength loss upon disturbance. Covers formation mechanism (salt leaching by fresh water), geographic occurrence, and key engineering hazards including brittleness and liquefaction-like behavior at small strains.
key_points: Quick clays form when formation water containing salts is replaced by fresh water, typically in marine depositional environments.
Disturbance from construction activities or seismic shaking can cause these clays to lose strength dramatically and become near-liquid.
Collapse occurs at relatively small strains due to their brittle nature.
Common locations include Norway, Canada, Sweden, Finland, Russia, and the United States; examples include Leda clay and Champlain Sea clay in Canada.
sections.applicability: Applies when investigating or designing foundations in areas with potentially sensitive marine-origin clays.

sections.title: Characteristics
sections.summary: Describes the defining engineering characteristics of quick clays: very high sensitivity, brittle stress-strain behavior, and the tendency to become liquid after disturbance. Explains that in their undisturbed state they can be relatively strong, but disturbance causes severe strength reduction.
sections.body: Quick clays are clays from marine origin that are characterized by their very high sensitivity or strength reduction upon disturbance. Quick clays are formed when the formation water containing salts is replaced with fresh water. Disturbance of these clays can be caused by construction activities or seismic ground shaking. In their undisturbed state, they are relatively strong. Following disturbance, they become very weak and possibly liquid. Because of their brittle nature, collapse occurs at relatively small strains. This type of clay is normally found in Norway, Canada, Sweden, Finland, Russia, the United States and other locations around the world. The Leda clay and Champlain Sea clay in Canada are examples of quick materials.
key_points: Quick clays originate in marine environments and are formed by replacement of saline formation water with fresh water.
They are relatively strong when undisturbed but become very weak or liquid upon disturbance.
Collapse at small strains due to brittleness makes them especially hazardous under dynamic or construction loading.
Globally distributed; notable examples are Leda clay and Champlain Sea clay in Canada.
sections.applicability: Applies when characterizing or classifying marine-origin clays in regions historically covered by post-glacial seas.

sections.title: Identification and Classification
sections.summary: Explains how quick clays are identified through measured sensitivity values greater than ~15 and distinctive strain-softening stress-strain curves. Defines sensitivity as the ratio of undrained shear strength in undisturbed to disturbed state, and notes that in situ liquidity index typically exceeds 1.
sections.body: Quick clays are readily recognized by measured sensitivities greater than about 15 and by the distinctive, strain-softening shape of their stress-strain curves from strength or compressibility tests. The sensitivity of clays is defined as the ratio of the undrained shear strength in the undisturbed state to that in the disturbed state. The in situ liquidity index of quick clays is typically above one, which means the water content is in excess of the liquid limit.
key_points: Sensitivity > ~15 is a primary identification criterion for quick clays.
Strain-softening stress-strain curves from strength or compressibility tests are a distinctive indicator.
Sensitivity = undrained shear strength (undisturbed) / undrained shear strength (disturbed).
In situ liquidity index typically > 1, meaning natural water content exceeds the liquid limit.
sections.applicability: Applies when testing or classifying suspect sensitive clays to determine if they qualify as quick clays.

sections.title: Other Materials and Considerations
sections.summary: Container section covering special or problematic soil and fill types beyond the main classification groups, including man-made fills, chemically reactive soils, lateritic soils, calcareous sands, and submarine soils. Each subsection addresses unique engineering challenges and relevant references.
key_points: This section addresses special materials and site conditions that require case-by-case engineering evaluation.
Topics include engineered vs. uncontrolled fills, corrosive and gas-generating soils, lateritic and calcareous sands, and marine sediments.
sections.applicability: Applies when site investigation reveals non-standard soil materials or conditions requiring specialized engineering consideration.

sections.title: Man-made Fills
sections.summary: Distinguishes between engineered fills (properly compacted to specified density and moisture) and uncontrolled fills (variable composition and placement). Engineered fills are suitable for foundations; uncontrolled fills have unpredictable properties and must be analyzed case-by-case. References NAVFAC DM 7.2.
sections.body:
Man-made fills can be divided into engineered fills and uncontrolled fills. Engineered fills are fills that were properly compacted to a specified density within a specified range of water contents. These fills are normally strong, have low compressibility, and are very favorable for building foundations. More detail on engineered fill can be found in NAVFAC DM 7.2 (NAVFAC 1982).

Uncontrolled fills are very problematic because these fills were placed under conditions that were not controlled and/or the materials that compose these fills were not controlled. These fills can be made from uncompacted soils and may contain deleterious building debris, old pavement, or concrete. Because of the variability of the materials and uncontrolled placement conditions, the engineering properties are very unpredictable and should be analyzed on a case-by-case basis.
key_points: Engineered fills are compacted to specified density and moisture range, yielding strong, low-compressibility material suitable for foundations.
Uncontrolled fills have highly variable composition (may include debris, old pavement, concrete) and unpredictable engineering properties.
Uncontrolled fills must be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.
NAVFAC DM 7.2 provides additional detail on engineered fill design.
sections.applicability: Applies when assessing existing fill materials at a site for foundation suitability or when designing new fill placements.

sections.title: Chemically Reactive Soils
sections.summary: Covers corrosion and gas generation hazards in chemically reactive soils, with criteria for high corrosion potential (pH, resistivity, sulfate/chloride concentration, etc.), mitigation strategies for steel and concrete foundations, and a table of corrosive soil environments in the U.S. per FHWA (2009) and AASHTO (2017).
sections.body:
For foundation construction, the main concerns related to chemically reactive soils are usually are corrosion and gas generation. Corrosive soils can be problematic when dealing with foundations, especially steel foundation systems. Potential for corrosion must be considered in the design of foundations compared to the design life of the structure. Protection systems can be used to reduce the corrosion rate. For concrete foundations, increasing the cover thickness over the steel, the use of additive treated concrete, or a specialized cement for this purpose can help mitigate the effect of corrosion on the reinforcement.

Corrosion potential is determined in terms of pH, resistivity, stray current activity, groundwater position, chemical analysis, etc. Based on this information, a compatible foundation treatment, (e.g., sulfate resistant concrete, lacquers, creosote, cathodic protection, etc.) can be prescribed. According to AASHTO (2017), a soil is considered have high corrosion potential if: (1) the resistivity is less than 2,000 ohm-cm, (2) the pH less than 5.5, (3) pH between 5.5 and 8.5 for soils with high organic content, (4) the sulfate concentration is greater than 1,000 ppm, (5) is subjected to mine or industrial drainage, or (6) the chloride concentration is greater than 500 ppm.

The location of the water table also influences the corrosion rate. Decker et al. (2008) observed higher corrosion rate on steel piles in the section located above the water table in the fluctuation zone.

FHWA (2009) presents an extensive study on the corrosion potential of soils focused on MSE walls. Table 1-23 indicates regions in the United States with soils with high potential for corrosion.

For gas concentration, organic matter content and field testing for gas are usually performed. If gas generation is expected, some form of venting system is designed. The potential presence of noxious or explosive gases should be considered during the construction excavations and tunneling.
key_points: Primary concerns for chemically reactive soils are corrosion of foundation materials (especially steel) and gas generation.
AASHTO (2017) high corrosion criteria: resistivity < 2,000 ohm-cm, pH < 5.5, sulfate > 1,000 ppm, chloride > 500 ppm, or exposure to mine/industrial drainage.
Mitigation for steel foundations includes cathodic protection, lacquers, and creosote; for concrete, increased cover, additive-treated concrete, or specialized cement.
Corrosion rate is higher above the water table fluctuation zone for steel piles (Decker et al. 2008).
Gas generation risk should be evaluated during excavations and tunneling; venting systems may be required.
Table 1-23 identifies U.S. regions with high corrosion potential soils per FHWA (2009).
sections.applicability: Applies when designing foundations in areas with potentially aggressive soils, including regions with acid-sulfate, sodic, organic, coastal, or industrial fill environments.

sections.title: Lateritic Soils
sections.summary: Describes lateritic soils found in tropical climates, characterized by high iron and aluminum content and rusty-red color. Notes engineering challenges including strength loss with time, high void ratio, permeability, aggregate deterioration, shrinkage cracks, and susceptibility to landslides and erratic foundation conditions.
sections.body: Lateritic soils are found in tropical climates throughout the world. These soils are rich in iron and aluminum. Because of the high iron content, most of these soils have a rusty-red color. Extensive weathering of the parent rock normally develops these soils. These soils can be problematic because of their loss in strength with time, high void ratio and permeability, aggregate deterioration, and shrinkage cracks. These soils tend to have shear strength characteristics between those of sands and silts. They are prone to cause landslides, have highly variable moisture content, and provide erratic conditions for foundations.
key_points: Lateritic soils form in tropical climates from extensive weathering and are rich in iron and aluminum, giving them a rusty-red color.
Engineering challenges include strength loss over time, high void ratio, high permeability, aggregate deterioration, and shrinkage cracking.
Shear strength characteristics fall between those of sands and silts.
These soils are prone to landslides, variable moisture content, and erratic foundation performance.
sections.applicability: Applies when investigating or designing foundations in tropical or subtropical regions where lateritic soils are prevalent.

sections.title: Calcareous Sands
sections.summary: Covers calcareous sands composed of marine organism skeletal remains with high carbonate content. Highlights their significant intra-particle voids, angular particle shape, and wide range of engineering properties controlled by cementation and structure. References ASTM Special Technical Publication for further information.
sections.body: Calcareous sands are composed mainly of the skeletal remains of marine organism having high carbonate content. These sands have significant intra-particle voids created by shells that have not broken yet and by the cavities in the corals. These sands are also characterized by having angular particles. The engineering properties of these sands vary over a wide range and are controlled by the cementation and the structure of the sand. More information on calcareous sands can be found in an ASTM Special Technical Publication on the topic (ASTM International 1981).
key_points: Calcareous sands consist mainly of skeletal remains of marine organisms with high carbonate content.
Significant intra-particle voids (from intact shells and coral cavities) and angular particles distinguish these sands.
Engineering properties vary widely and are governed by cementation degree and sand structure.
ASTM International (1981) Special Technical Publication provides additional technical detail.
sections.applicability: Applies when characterizing or designing foundations in coastal or offshore areas where calcareous sands are present.

sections.title: Submarine Soils
sections.summary: Describes ocean floor topography, distribution of marine sediments, and key engineering differences between marine and terrestrial sediments. Covers normally consolidated, overconsolidated, and underconsolidated states of marine sediments, and discusses effects of pressure, salinity, and hydrodynamic forcing on sediment engineering behavior.
sections.body:
Ocean environments contains the following main topographic features: (1) the continental margin including the continental shelf fringing the coast and the continental slope; (2) the continental rise; and (3) the abyssal plains with local seamounts and trenches (Randolph and Gourvenec 2011). The distribution of marine sediments along those geomorphological regions varies with thickest sediment deposits being mostly near continents and thinnest on recently formed mid-oceanic ridges. Continental margins contain almost 75% of marine sediments, while only representing 20% of the seabed area. The continental rise is also considered a depositional feature with sediment thickness reaching locally up to 1.6 km (Randolph and Gourvenec 2011).

Marine sediments are either terrigenous (i.e. transported from land to the ocean), or pelagic (i.e. settled through the water column). Coastal and nearshore zones are dominated by terrigenous sediments. Terrigenous sediments are often granular silicate minerals formed from erosion (lithogenous). Pelagic sediments are often finer and derived from insoluble remains of marine organisms. Poulos (1988) presented samples from abyssal plain and hill environments and found that most samples from abyssal plains and hills characterized as clayey silt to clay. Ocean sediment mapping also revealed that deep ocean floors are widely covered with calcareous ooze that classified as mostly silty clay (Poulos 1988).

Marine sediments that were deposited slowly and remained undisturbed from physical, chemical, benthic biogenic, and/or anthropogenic processes are commonly normally consolidated. Overconsolidated sediments can result from glaciation, recent sediment erosion, or submarine landslides. Underconsolidated marine sediments can follow from rapid sedimentation events and recent sediment dynamics, as well as from benthic biogenic processes, amongst others. More information on the stress states of marine sediments can be found in Randolph and Gourvenec (2011).

The following key differences between marine and terrestrial sediments can be listed:
• Environmental conditions cover a wider range of pressures (depending on water depth) and temperature and can affect the engineering behavior of marine sediments, particularly in deep ocean environments.
• Oceans feature saline water. Local salinity may affect the engineering behavior, particularly of clays.
• Hydrodynamic conditions (i.e., waves, tides, currents) vary on spatial and temporal scales, particularly in nearshore environments and on the continental shelf. Hydrodynamic forcing can exert stresses onto the seabed and change pore pressures. It also drives sediment dynamics, potentially leading to complex sediment dynamics including erosion, transport, and deposition, and resulting in geomorphodynamics including the formation, destruction, and migration of bedforms on scales of centimeters to hundreds of meters. These processes affect sediment composition, texture, and thus, engineering properties.
key_points: Continental margins hold ~75% of marine sediments but represent only 20% of seabed area; sediment thickness on the continental rise can reach 1.6 km.
Marine sediments are terrigenous (land-derived, often granular) or pelagic (ocean-settled, often finer clay-sized material).
Deep ocean floors are widely covered with calcareous ooze classified mostly as silty clay.
Slowly deposited undisturbed marine sediments are typically normally consolidated; overconsolidation can result from glaciation, erosion, or submarine landslides.
Key differences from terrestrial sediments: wider pressure/temperature range, saline pore water, and hydrodynamic forcing affecting stress, pore pressure, and sediment dynamics.
Hydrodynamic processes drive bedform formation on scales of centimeters to hundreds of meters, affecting composition, texture, and engineering properties.
sections.applicability: Applies when conducting geotechnical investigations or foundation design for offshore, nearshore, or deep ocean structures.

Topics covered include soil classification, rock description and classification, expansive and collapsing soils, frost susceptibility, limestone/karst conditions, lateritic soils, and submarine soils, with specific citations to key industry references.

sections.title: Notation
sections.summary: Defines all symbols and abbreviations used throughout Chapter 1. Covers index properties (Cu, Cc, D10, D30, D60, LL, PL, PI, EI, GI), rock classification parameters (GSI, RMR, RQD), rock point load test variables (d, De, F, P), and expansion index test quantities (Hi, ΔH), providing a quick reference for interpreting equations and tables in the chapter.
sections.body:
Symbol | Description
Cu | Coefficient of uniformity
Cc | Coefficient of curvature
d | Distance between the loaded points in rock point load test
De | Equivalent core diameter
D10 | Particle size diameter corresponding to 10% passing
D30 | Particle-size diameter corresponding to 30% passing
D60 | Particle-size diameter corresponding to 60% passing
EI | Expansion index
F | Percentage passing a No. 200 (75 μm) sieve (only considering the particles passing a 3-inch sieve)
F | Size correction factor for rock point load test
GI | Group index
GSI | Geological strength index
Hi | Initial height of the test specimen in the expansion index test
LL | Liquid limit of the soil
P | Applied force at failure
PI | Plasticity index of the soil
PL | Plastic limit of the soil
RMR | Rock mass rating
RQD | Rock quality designation
∆H | Change in height during the expansion index test
key_points: Cu and Cc define grain-size distribution curve shape for soil classification.
D10, D30, and D60 are the particle-size diameters at 10%, 30%, and 60% passing, used to compute Cu and Cc.
LL, PL, and PI are Atterberg limits used in fine-grained soil classification and plasticity assessment.
EI (Expansion Index), Hi, and ΔH are specific to the expansion index test for expansive soil identification.
RQD, RMR, and GSI are rock quality and classification indices referenced in the rock description sections.
d, De, F, and P relate to the rock point load test strength assessment.
GI (Group Index) is used in the AASHTO soil classification system.
